scenes.narration: What if one of the world's most important industries depended on an island smaller than Switzerland?
Taiwan covers about 36,000 square kilometers. Yet most of the world's most advanced chips are made right here.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: So how did a small island become the center of chipmaking? It matters because almost everything we use now runs on chips, and someone has to make them.
For a long time, the chip business had one rule. If you designed chips, you also built the factory that made them, called a fab. And fabs were brutally expensive. So only giants could play.

In 1987, with backing from Taiwan's government and the Dutch company Philips, a new company called TSMC tried something different. It would design nothing. It would only manufacture chips, for anyone. It became the world's first dedicated chip foundry. That one idea rewired the industry. A small team with a great design no longer needed its own factory. Nvidia, founded in 1993, became one of those designers, and so did Apple and AMD. They focus on design and send their blueprints to Taiwan. The timeline turned into a network, and Taiwan sat at the center of it.

Today TSMC takes about 72 percent of all the revenue earned by the world's top ten contract chipmakers. In twenty twenty-five alone, it brought in 122 billion dollars. And at the end of that year, 77 percent of its wafer revenue came from its most advanced processes, seven nanometers and smaller. Taiwan didn't just join the industry. It took over the hardest part of it.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: But if the idea was that simple, why didn't everyone copy it?

keyframes.label: If the idea was that simple

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Why can't every country just build its own chip factories? If they could, Taiwan would not be special at all.

Let me draw what it takes. First, engineers design the chip, billions of tiny switches. Then a fab prints that design onto a silicon wafer, layer after layer, using light. Then the wafer is cut into chips, packaged with memory, and tested. Every step has to be close to perfect.

Here is the first obstacle. To print the smallest features, a fab needs extreme ultraviolet lithography machines. Only one company in the world makes them, the Dutch firm A S M L. In twenty twenty-five, it shipped 48 of them.

And owning the machines is not enough. The real secret is yield, the share of chips on each wafer that actually work. Raising yield takes years of practice, thousands of engineers, and endless learning from mistakes. A brand-new factory, even with the very same machines, can take a long time to match the yields of an experienced one. That know-how is hard to buy, and even harder to copy.

Then there is the money. TSMC planned to spend more than 50 billion dollars on factories and equipment in twenty twenty-six alone. Across the industry, chipmakers are expected to invest about 2.3 trillion dollars in new fabs between twenty twenty-four and twenty thirty-two.

Taiwan does not make most of the world's chips. In twenty twenty-two it had 18 percent of all chipmaking capacity, less than China. But for the most advanced logic chips, below ten nanometers, Taiwan had 69 percent. South Korea had 31 percent. The United States had none.

And chips are not one market. Memory is a different game, led by South Korea, which had about half of the world's DRAM capacity. Advanced packaging, the step that joins chips and memory, has become a bottleneck of its own. So Taiwan's edge is narrow, but it sits at the very top.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Which raises the next question. Who depends on that top?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: So who actually depends on Taiwan? It matters because dependence is where economic power, and economic risk, come from.

Let me draw it. Here is Taiwan. And here, across the Pacific, is California, home to Nvidia, Apple and AMD. They design chips, but they don't make their most advanced chips themselves. TSMC does. So the lines run from California to Taiwan, and back again as finished chips.

How concentrated is it? In twenty twenty-five, TSMC's largest customer alone made up 19 percent of its revenue, and the second largest 17 percent. Nvidia's chief executive has said Nvidia is the biggest, and the second is widely reported to be Apple. But notice that this dependence runs both ways. TSMC needs its biggest customers almost as much as they need TSMC.

Now follow the chips further. Cloud companies in the United States, Europe and Asia fill their data centers with AI chips made in Taiwan. Phone makers, PC makers and carmakers buy chips too. In twenty twenty-five, Taiwan's exports hit a record 640 billion dollars, up 35 percent in a single year.

Here is the key distinction. Companies that design chips depend on the companies that make them. And the makers depend on Dutch machines, Japanese materials and American design software. Everyone depends on someone.

But not every industry depends on Taiwan equally. A cutting-edge AI chip or a new phone processor needs the most advanced factories, and that is where Taiwan dominates. A car or a washing machine mostly uses older, simpler chips that are made in many countries. Even so, a missing cheap chip can still stop a car factory.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: So what would happen if the flow of chips from Taiwan were suddenly interrupted?

keyframes.label: What if the flow of chips

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Here is a thought experiment. What if chip shipments from Taiwan were seriously disrupted? To be clear, this is a hypothetical scenario, not a prediction.

We do have one real clue. In twenty twenty-one, a chip shortage caused by the pandemic, not by Taiwan, hit carmakers hard. One forecast put the cost to the global auto industry at 210 billion dollars in lost revenue, and 7.7 million vehicles that were never built.

Now imagine a disruption at the source. Advanced chip supply stops. New phones and computers slip. Cloud companies can't add AI servers. Carmakers idle their lines. Prices rise, and the shock spreads to industries that never thought of themselves as tech. A shortage of the most advanced chips would be very hard to replace quickly, because the alternative factories simply don't exist yet at that scale.

Let me draw that chain. Taiwan's fabs. Then packaging. Then the device makers. Then the stores and the data centers. Now break the very first link, and watch the shock travel down the line. Every box after the break turns red.

scenes.visual_objective: Side-by-side figures count up; bars rise
scenes.narration: How big could it get? In twenty twenty-four, Bloomberg Economics estimated that a war over Taiwan could cut world output by about 10 percent in the first year, about 10 trillion dollars. Even a blockade could cost about 5 percent. Bloomberg stresses these are scenarios, and they depend heavily on assumptions.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: Numbers like that explain why governments are now racing to make chips at home.

keyframes.label: explain the race to make chips at home

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Can the world spread the risk? It matters because diversification is expensive, and it is slow.

Let's map the race. America's CHIPS Act offers about 53 billion dollars for semiconductors, 39 billion dollars of it for manufacturing. TSMC plans to invest 165 billion dollars in Arizona. In Japan, its Kumamoto venture costs more than 20 billion dollars.

In Germany, a TSMC joint venture is rising in Dresden, and Europe wants 20 percent of global chip production by twenty thirty. South Korea keeps pouring money into memory and its own foundries. And Taiwan keeps building its newest fabs at home.

But here is the limit. Even with all this spending, the forecast from the industry's own trade group and Boston Consulting Group still has Taiwan holding 47 percent of advanced logic capacity in twenty thirty-two, with the United States at 28 percent. Diversification reduces the risk. It doesn't remove it.

Why so slow? Because the hard part isn't the building. It is the engineers, the suppliers, and the years of yield learning that come with them. Taiwan has spent decades on that. A new fab abroad can be built in a few years. Building the whole ecosystem around it takes much longer.

Taiwan matters not because it makes every chip, but because it makes the hardest ones, at a scale nobody else has matched. An island smaller than Switzerland ended up holding one of the most important keys to the global economy. Its strength is also the world's weak point: so much of the cutting edge in one place. And that is why the whole world is watching it.
